Takeaways Up Front

1. The Pentagon released 43 more UFO files in its eighth batch under Trump’s disclosure order.

2. A 2009 contractor report proposed a buried North Las Vegas vault for hardware and biological samples.

3. A 2023 radar event over the western U.S. implies at least 1,650 mph, if it tracked one object.

The Pentagon released 43 more files on unidentified anomalous phenomena on Nov. 20, among them a 538-page contractor report from 2009 that laid out plans for a buried, camouflaged vault in North Las Vegas to hold recovered hardware and biological samples.

The files are the eighth batch published under the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters, which the Department of War began populating in May after President Donald Trump directed agencies to release their UFO records. Most of the new material consists of Air Force and CIA documents from the 1950s.

The vault plan appears in a report that Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, or BAASS, wrote in July 2009 to summarize its first 10 months of work for the Defense Intelligence Agency. Robert Bigelow’s aerospace company set up BAASS for the agency’s Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program, which studied potential aerospace threats more than 40 years into the future, and won the contract as the only bidder. 

BAASS had made it a priority to pursue recovered hardware and biological samples from companies, private individuals and groups, including some in Brazil, but had no secure place to keep them. 

In May 2009, its administrator noted the lack of a facility for “exotic material or tissue” and designed an underground vault at the Bigelow Aerospace site in North Las Vegas, which was already ringed by razor wire and guarded around the clock by armed retired and serving military personnel.

The plans called for a 5,000-square-foot vault under 15 to 20 feet of earth, with walls, ceiling and floor 3 feet thick. A concrete tunnel would lead to it through several security doors, at least one of them a thick steel vault door. Anything protruding above ground was to be “extensively camouflaged.”

BAASS expected the vault to be ready by late 2009 or early 2010 and promised details in an August 2009 monthly report that is not among the released files. Whether it was ever built is unclear, since later BAASS reports released by the Pentagon never mention it again.

Although a copy leaked online last year, the release marks the first time the Pentagon has published the report.

The batch also includes the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office’s preliminary analysis of a 2023 radar event over the western United States, where a civilian air-surveillance radar recorded eight returns in 84 seconds at altitudes the office estimated between 55,000 and 70,000 feet. 

Treated as one object, the returns would span about 38.5 miles, implying an average ground speed of at least 1,650 mph. The office said the available data could not show that all eight detections came from a single object, so the event remains unresolved.

Three military video clips from the Middle East, filed with the same office, show white dots crossing the screen, with file names pointing to events in 2020, 2023 and 2026.

The older records include a 16-page CIA file from the fall of 1952, when Director of Central Intelligence Walter Bedell Smith told the Psychological Strategy Board he was sending the National Security Council a proposal on “flying saucers.” 

The proposal concluded that the problems connected with unidentified flying objects “appear to have implications for psychological warfare as well as for intelligence and operations.” Smith asked the board to discuss “the possible offensive or defensive utilization of these phenomena for psychological warfare purposes.”

The attached CIA study counted about 1,500 official sightings since 1947, including 250 in July 1952 alone. The Air Force carried 20% of the total as unexplained, a share that rose to 28% for reports received in 1952. Its analysts expected 10% to stay unexplained even with full information, a residue the study called “incredible reports from credible observers.”

The agency wanted to know whether any of the objects could be controlled or predicted for military or psychological use, how much Soviet scientists knew about them and whether Moscow could exploit them against the United States. It described the Soviet press’s silence on flying saucers as “in itself provocative.” 

Consultants at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology told CIA officers the answers probably lay at the edge of existing knowledge in atmospherics, ionization and extraterrestrial phenomena, adding that nuclear waste products might also be a factor.

A follow-up CIA memo on Oct. 13, 1952, concluded that the agency had no basis yet for psychological warfare planners to use the phenomena. It recommended a National Intelligence Estimate before any public policy aimed at calming public concern.

SOFX has followed the earlier releases, from the first 162 files in May to an AC-130J encounter over the Gulf of Oman in the fifth batch. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the department and its partner agencies are already working on the next release.
